summary: Describes the View-based Access Control Model for SNMP, with procedures for controlling access to management information. It also includes a MIB for remotely managing its configuration. It was replaced by RFC 2275.

eli5.summary: It decides which people can look at, or change, which pieces of a device's information, like keys that open only some doors.

questions: how does snmp access control work
how does vacm use security levels
subtitle: Controlling who can access which parts of a managed system's information.

tldr.problem: Network management systems need to control which managers can read or modify which pieces of information on managed devices, varying by the level of security used.
tldr.mechanism: VACM maps security principals (identified by model and name) to groups, then defines which groups can read, write, or send notifications about objects in particular contexts, using the security level to grant or deny access.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can granularly restrict access without writing application code, using three tables to configure groups, access rules, and which object subtrees are visible. RFC 2275 replaced this with a similar model updated for modern SNMP.

today: RFC 2265 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 2275, which provides a nearly identical model for modern SNMPv3 deployments. VACM remains the standard way to implement access control in SNMP, and the model has not been fundamentally changed since 1998.

sections.title: Why SNMP Needs Access Control
sections.content:
In any network management system, not all managers need access to all information. Some operators should only read performance data. Others with higher security clearance and stronger authentication might write configuration changes. Still others should not see sensitive system details at all. The View-based Access Control Model (VACM) defines how an SNMP engine enforces these restrictions without requiring changes to each management application.

VACM is one of two required subsystems in SNMPv3, working alongside the security model (which handles authentication and encryption). Where the security model verifies that a message came from a legitimate user, VACM decides what that user is allowed to do with the information inside.
sections.eli5: Just like a building has different security levels for different rooms, a network device has different access levels for different information. VACM is the bouncer at each door, checking your credentials.

sections.title: The Five Key Concepts
sections.content:
VACM is built on five concepts that work together:

Groups bundle security principals with the same access rights. A group can contain many users (securityNames) with the same securityModel, like all the read-only operators on a device.

Security Levels distinguish between unauthenticated access (noAuthNoPriv), authenticated but unencrypted (authNoPriv), and authenticated and encrypted (authPriv). Higher levels open more access doors.

Contexts are collections of management information on a device. A device might have a default context, plus contexts for individual virtual machines or network partitions, each isolated from the others.

MIB Views are subsets of the management information in a context. A view is defined as a union of object subtrees to include, minus any subtrees to exclude, using a bit mask to allow wildcards.

Access Policy connects these: a group, within a context, using a specific securityModel and securityLevel, is allowed to read, write, or send notifications about objects in specified MIB views.
sections.eli5: To give someone access, five things must match up: who you are (group), what time of day it is (security level), where the information is (context), what subset of information you can see (view), and what you can do with it (read, write, or notify).

sections.title: The Access Check Procedure
sections.content:
When an SNMP command responder receives a request or when a notification originator is about to send a notification, the engine calls the access control module to decide if the action is allowed. The request passes six pieces of information: the securityModel and securityName (who), the securityLevel (how strongly authenticated), the contextName (where), the viewType (read, write, or notify), and the variableName (which object).

The engine then follows a multi-step process. First, it looks up the group that corresponds to the securityModel and securityName. If no group is found, access is denied immediately. Second, it finds the access control entry for that group, context, securityModel, and securityLevel. If no entry matches, access is denied. Third, it selects the appropriate MIB view (read, write, or notify) from that entry. If the view is empty, access is denied. Finally, it checks whether the requested object is contained in the view, using the view subtrees and their masks to determine inclusion or exclusion. If the object is in the view, access is allowed; otherwise it is denied.
sections.eli5: The bouncer asks five questions: Are you a known group? Is your security level high enough? Are you in the right place? Is this object on the list you can see? If all answers are yes, the door opens.

sections.title: Configuration Tables
sections.content:
VACM defines a MIB module with three main tables for remote configuration via SNMP itself. The vacmSecurityToGroupTable maps each combination of securityModel and securityName to a groupName. This is the first lookup in the access check. The vacmAccessTable defines the access policy: for each group, contextName, securityModel, and securityLevel, it specifies the read-view, write-view, and notify-view names. It also allows matching a context prefix instead of the exact context name, enabling flexible context namespacing. The vacmViewTreeFamilyTable defines which object subtrees are included in or excluded from each named view. Each entry specifies a subtree OID, a bit mask indicating which sub-identifiers must match, and whether the subtree is included or excluded from the view.

The tables also include storage type and row status objects to control persistence and row creation. A spin-lock object helps prevent collisions when multiple managers configure views concurrently.
sections.eli5: The MIB has three phone books: one to look up your group, one to look up your access rights, and one to look up which objects are in each view.

sections.title: Using VACM Safely
sections.content: The RFC defines several best practices for deploying VACM. When adding or removing view subtrees, follow the recommended order to avoid accidentally granting access during the transition: create excluded subtrees before included ones, and delete included before excluded. The securityLevel index in the access table should be used to carefully separate access for different security levels, since the group-to-securityName mapping does not consider security level. Implementing instance-level access control (restricting access not just to object types but to specific instances) can have performance costs, so managers should avoid unnecessary instance-level granularity. The default installation parameters in the RFC define recommended initial views like internet (all management information) and restricted (system, SNMP, and engine statistics) for unauthenticated access.
sections.eli5: Be careful when adding or removing doors; do it in the right order so no one sneaks through. Match the person's security level carefully, not just their group. And if you do instance-level access control, your device will be slower.
